title: Walk through every JVM memory area in detail: Heap (Young = Eden+S0+S1, Old), Metaspace (native), Stack (per-thread), Code Cache (JIT), and Direct/off-heap memory — what each stores and how it is bounded (-Xms/-Xmx/-Xss/-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize/-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize/-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize).
shortTitle: Walk through every JVM memory area in detail and how each is bounded.

s1_definition.profdef: The Java virtual machine divides memory into several distinct regions. The heap holds all objects and is split into the Young generation (Eden plus two Survivor spaces, S0 and S1) and the Old generation. Metaspace, which lives in native memory outside the heap, holds class metadata. Each thread has its own stack holding stack frames for method calls. The Code Cache stores native machine code produced by the just-in-time compiler. Direct, or off-heap, memory holds buffers allocated outside the heap, typically for input and output. Each region is bounded by its own flags: `-Xms` and `-Xmx` size the heap, `-Xss` sizes each thread stack, `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` caps Metaspace, `-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize` caps the Code Cache, and `-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize` caps direct memory.
s1_definition.analogy: Picture National Bank of India's main building. The heap is the giant main vault where all the money folders (objects) live; it has a busy front section for new folders (Young generation) and a deep back section for folders that have survived a long time (Old generation). Metaspace is a separate records room next door holding the blueprints of every folder type (class metadata). Each teller has their own small desk with a stack of forms they are currently working on (the thread stack). The Code Cache is a workshop where frequently used procedures are turned into fast machine tools (compiled code). Direct memory is an external loading dock for bulk cash shipments that bypass the main vault. Every room has a posted maximum capacity sign (the tuning flags).
s1_definition.oneliner: The JVM splits memory into the heap for objects (Young plus Old), native Metaspace for class metadata, a per-thread stack for frames, the Code Cache for JIT-compiled code, and direct memory for off-heap buffers, each bounded by its own flag.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Java virtual machine divides memory into several distinct regions. The heap holds all objects and is split into the Young generation (Eden plus two Survivor spaces, S0 and S1) and the Old generation. Metaspace, which lives in native memory outside the heap, holds class metadata. Each thread has its own stack holding stack frames for method calls. The Code Cache stores native machine code produced by the just-in-time compiler. Direct, or off-heap, memory holds buffers allocated outside the heap, typically for input and output. Each region is bounded by its own flags: `-Xms` and `-Xmx` size the heap, `-Xss` sizes each thread stack, `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize` caps Metaspace, `-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize` caps the Code Cache, and `-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize` caps direct memory.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Picture National Bank of India's main building. The heap is the giant main vault where all the money folders (objects) live; it has a busy front section for new folders (Young generation) and a deep back section for folders that have survived a long time (Old generation). Metaspace is a separate records room next door holding the blueprints of every folder type (class metadata). Each teller has their own small desk with a stack of forms they are currently working on (the thread stack). The Code Cache is a workshop where frequently used procedures are turned into fast machine tools (compiled code). Direct memory is an external loading dock for bulk cash shipments that bypass the main vault. Every room has a posted maximum capacity sign (the tuning flags).

**One line to remember:** The JVM splits memory into the heap for objects (Young plus Old), native Metaspace for class metadata, a per-thread stack for frames, the Code Cache for JIT-compiled code, and direct memory for off-heap buffers, each bounded by its own flag.

sections.s2_technical:
The heap is the largest region and is shared by all threads. It stores every object and array you create. It is generational: the Young generation holds newly created, short-lived objects and is itself divided into Eden, where objects are first allocated, and two equal Survivor spaces named S0 and S1 that hold objects surviving one or more minor collections. The Old generation, sometimes called Tenured, holds objects that have survived long enough to be promoted. The heap's starting and maximum sizes are set with `-Xms` and `-Xmx`, for example `-Xms2g -Xmx2g`, and setting them equal avoids runtime resizing pauses. Most garbage collection activity happens here, and a `java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space` means the heap genuinely filled up with reachable objects.

Metaspace holds class metadata: the structure of each loaded class, its method bytecode, field layout, and constant pool. Crucially, since Java 8 this lives in native memory, not the heap, so it grows with the operating system's memory rather than competing with your objects. By default it is unbounded and grows as needed, which can exhaust native memory if an application leaks class loaders; you cap it with `-XX:MaxMetaspaceSize`. A small example of why this matters in banking is an application server that hot-deploys many versions of a service; each deploy loads a new set of classes, and without Metaspace being reclaimed you get `OutOfMemoryError: Metaspace`.

Each thread gets its own stack, allocated when the thread starts, holding one frame per active method call. A frame stores that method's local variables, operand stack, and the return address. Because each recursive or nested call pushes a frame, very deep call chains overflow the stack with a `StackOverflowError`. The per-thread stack size is set with `-Xss`, for example `-Xss512k`; larger stacks allow deeper recursion but each thread then consumes more memory, which limits how many threads you can create. The Program Counter register, a tiny per-thread area holding the address of the current instruction, and the native method stack for native calls round out the per-thread memory.

The Code Cache stores native machine code that the just-in-time compiler produces from hot bytecode. As methods run often, the JIT compiles them to fast native code kept here; if the Code Cache fills, the JIT stops compiling and performance quietly degrades to interpreted speed. It is bounded with `-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize`. Direct, or off-heap, memory is allocated outside the heap, typically through `ByteBuffer.allocateDirect` or by libraries like Netty, and is used for high-performance input and output because it avoids a copy between the heap and the operating system. It is not collected by the normal garbage collector in the same way; it is freed when its backing object is collected and a Cleaner runs. You cap it with `-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize`. A senior nuance is that a container's memory limit counts all of these, heap plus Metaspace plus thread stacks plus Code Cache plus direct memory, so sizing only `-Xmx` and ignoring the rest is how a Java process gets killed by the operating system even though the heap looks fine, which is a very common production incident.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India's transfer service runs in a container with a hard memory limit. The team sized only the heap with `-Xmx` and the container kept getting killed. This is exactly why you must understand every memory area, because the container limit counts heap plus Metaspace plus thread stacks plus Code Cache plus direct memory, not just the heap.

Problem 2 — The service allocates objects for each transfer (heap), spawns worker threads (stacks), loads many classes (Metaspace), compiles hot methods (Code Cache), and uses direct buffers for the ledger file (off-heap). The team wanted to observe and bound each region separately. This is exactly what the memory flags do.

In the mini-project we build a small demo that deliberately touches each region: allocating transfer objects on the heap, recursing to use the stack, reading the JVM's memory beans to report heap and non-heap usage, and allocating a direct ByteBuffer. The demo logs each region's usage so the connection between code and memory area is visible.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile the demo
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/jvmmem/JvmMemoryAreasDemo.java

# Run with explicit bounds for EACH memory area
java -Xms256m -Xmx256m \
     -Xss512k \
     -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=128m \
     -XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize=64m \
     -XX:MaxDirectMemorySize=64m \
     -cp out com.bank.jvmmem.JvmMemoryAreasDemo

# Observe native memory breakdown (which region is growing)
java -XX:NativeMemoryTracking=summary -Xms256m -Xmx256m \
     -cp out com.bank.jvmmem.JvmMemoryAreasDemo
# then: jcmd <pid> VM.native_memory summary
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a startup report, then one hundred thousand Account allocations, a recursion of depth five hundred, and an eight-megabyte direct buffer.

Step 1: At startup the reporter reads the memory beans. Heap usage is low and non-heap already has several megabytes because the JVM's own classes are loaded into Metaspace and some methods are compiled into the Code Cache.

Step 2: The loop creates one hundred thousand Account objects. Each is first allocated in Eden inside the Young generation. As Eden fills, minor collections move survivors into a Survivor space, and long-lived ones are eventually promoted to the Old generation. The second report shows heap usage risen sharply.

Step 3: The recursion pushes five hundred stack frames onto the current thread's stack, each frame holding the method's parameters and return address. The frames unwind as the calls return. This never touches the heap; it lives entirely in the per-thread stack bounded by the stack size flag.

Step 4: The direct ByteBuffer allocates eight megabytes outside the heap in native memory. The report after it shows heap barely changed, because the buffer's bytes are off-heap, while the operating system sees the process using more memory.

Step 5: References are kept alive so the reports reflect real usage rather than collected objects.

```text
[INFO] [startup] HEAP used=3MB (max 256MB), NON-HEAP used=7MB (Metaspace + Code Cache)
[INFO] allocated 100000 accounts on the HEAP
[INFO] [after heap allocation] HEAP used=28MB (max 256MB), NON-HEAP used=9MB (Metaspace + Code Cache)
[INFO] stack recursion reached depth 500
[INFO] allocated 8MB DIRECT buffer; first long = 1000000
[INFO] [after direct buffer] HEAP used=28MB (max 256MB), NON-HEAP used=9MB (Metaspace + Code Cache)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  JVM Process Memory
    │
    ├─ HEAP (-Xms/-Xmx)                 shared by all threads
    │    ├─ Young Generation
    │    │    ├─ Eden        ← new Account objects land here
    │    │    ├─ S0 (Survivor)
    │    │    └─ S1 (Survivor)
    │    └─ Old Generation   ← promoted long-lived objects
    │
    ├─ Metaspace (NATIVE, -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize)   class metadata
    ├─ Thread Stacks (-Xss, one PER thread)       sumDepth frames
    │    └─ frame: locals + operand stack + return addr
    ├─ PC Register (per thread)                   current instruction
    ├─ Code Cache (-XX:ReservedCodeCacheSize)     JIT native code
    └─ Direct / off-heap (-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize) 8MB ByteBuffer

  Container limit = HEAP + Metaspace + Stacks + Code Cache + Direct
```
sections.s5c_hld:
```text
  ═══ HLD — Sizing a Banking Service's JVM in Kubernetes ═══

  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Pod memory limit = 1Gi (cgroup hard cap)          │
  │                                                   │
  │  JVM process must fit the WHOLE cap:              │
  │   ┌───────────────┐  -Xmx 512m   (heap)          │
  │   │ Heap          │                               │
  │   ├───────────────┤  MaxMetaspaceSize 128m        │
  │   │ Metaspace     │                               │
  │   ├───────────────┤  threads × -Xss (e.g. 200×1m) │
  │   │ Thread stacks │                               │
  │   ├───────────────┤  ReservedCodeCacheSize 64m    │
  │   │ Code Cache    │                               │
  │   ├───────────────┤  MaxDirectMemorySize 128m     │
  │   │ Direct/off-heap│                              │
  │   └───────────────┘  + JVM overhead                │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  If sum > limit → Kubernetes OOMKilled (not a heap OOM).
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```text
  ═══ LLD — Memory Areas and Their Flags ═══

  Area          Stores                     Bound by            Error
  ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
  Heap Young    new objects (Eden+S0+S1)   -Xmx (shared)       heap space
  Heap Old      promoted objects           -Xmx (shared)       heap space
  Metaspace     class metadata (native)    MaxMetaspaceSize    Metaspace
  Thread stack  frames per method call     -Xss (per thread)   StackOverflow
  PC register   current instr addr         (tiny, per thread)  —
  Code Cache    JIT native code            ReservedCodeCacheSize  (JIT stops)
  Direct mem    off-heap NIO buffers       MaxDirectMemorySize Direct buffer OOM

  Thread-safety: heap + Metaspace + Code Cache are SHARED;
                 stack + PC register are PER-THREAD (no sharing).

  MemoryReporter contract:
    getHeapMemoryUsage()    → Young + Old
    getNonHeapMemoryUsage() → Metaspace + Code Cache
    (direct memory tracked via NativeMemoryTracking / BufferPoolMXBean)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The Java virtual machine divides its memory into several distinct regions, and I like to walk through each with what it stores and how it is bounded. The largest is the heap, shared by all threads, which holds every object and array. The heap is generational: the Young generation holds newly created, short-lived objects and is itself split into Eden, where objects are first allocated, and two equal Survivor spaces, S0 and S1, that hold objects surviving minor collections, while the Old generation holds objects that have lived long enough to be promoted. I size the heap with dash Xms for the initial size and dash Xmx for the maximum, and I usually set them equal to avoid runtime resizing pauses. A Java heap space out-of-memory error means the heap genuinely filled with reachable objects.

Next is Metaspace, which holds class metadata, meaning the structure of each loaded class, its method bytecode, field layout, and constant pool. The key point since Java 8 is that Metaspace lives in native memory outside the heap, so it grows with operating-system memory rather than competing with your objects, and by default it is unbounded unless I cap it with MaxMetaspaceSize. This matters in an application server that hot-deploys many versions of a service, because leaking class loaders produces a Metaspace out-of-memory error. Then there is the per-thread stack, allocated when a thread starts, holding one frame per active method call, where each frame stores that method's local variables, operand stack, and return address. Deep recursion overflows it with a StackOverflowError, and I size it with dash Xss, keeping in mind that a bigger stack per thread means fewer threads overall.

The Code Cache stores the native machine code the just-in-time compiler produces from hot methods, and if it fills, the JIT stops compiling and performance quietly drops back toward interpreted speed; I bound it with ReservedCodeCacheSize. Finally there is direct, or off-heap, memory, allocated outside the heap through things like a direct ByteBuffer or Netty, used for high-performance input and output because it avoids copying between the heap and the operating system, and I cap it with MaxDirectMemorySize. There is also the tiny per-thread program counter register that tracks the current instruction.

The senior lesson I always close with, because it has caused real production incidents on my teams, is that a container's memory limit counts all of these together: heap plus Metaspace plus thread stacks plus Code Cache plus direct memory, plus some JVM overhead. If I size only dash Xmx and ignore the rest, the Java process can be killed by the operating system with an OOMKilled even though the heap looks perfectly healthy, and that failure looks nothing like a normal Java heap out-of-memory error. So when I size a banking service in Kubernetes, I budget every region against the pod limit, and I use Native Memory Tracking to see which region is actually growing.
